s.line: The Cowardly Lion was much pleased to hear that the Wicked Witch had been melted by a bucket of water,
s.note: נָמַסָּה = "she melted", nif'al of the doubled root מ־ס־ס, where the second and third letters are the same (masculine נָמַס). Hebrew says "she melted because of a bucket" and does not use the English passive "was melted by". You'll hear נָמֵס for ice or chocolate: הַשּׁוֹקוֹלָד נָמֵס בַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ.

s.line: and Dorothy at once unlocked the gate of his prison and set him free.
s.note: שִׁחְרֵר = to set free, release: a four-letter root in pi'el. Common relatives: שִׁחְרוּר (liberation; also release from prison or discharge from the army) and מְשֻׁחְרָר (a discharged soldier). In the news: הָאָסִיר שֻׁחְרַר (the prisoner was released).

s.line: They went in together to the castle,
where Dorothy’s first act was to call all the Winkies together and tell them that they were no longer slaves.
s.note: נִכְנַס (went in) and כִּנֵּס (gathered people together) share the root כ־נ־ס: nif'al "to enter", pi'el "to bring together". כֶּנֶס is a conference, and the כְּנֶסֶת is Israel's parliament. כְּבָר לֹא = "no longer, not any more": אֲנִי כְּבָר לֹא גָּר שָׁם.

s.line: There was great rejoicing among the yellow Winkies, for they had been made to work hard during many years for the Wicked Witch,
s.note: הֻכְרְחוּ = "they were forced", hof'al: the passive of hif'il הִכְרִיחַ (to force someone). Pattern: הִכְרִיחַ → הֻכְרַח, like הִזְמִין invited → הֻזְמַן was invited. From the same root: הֶכְרֵחִי = necessary, בְּהֶכְרֵחַ = necessarily.

s.line: who had always treated them with great cruelty.
s.note: הִתְיַחֵס אֶל = to treat someone (in a certain way), with אֶל / לְ: הוּא מִתְיַחֵס אֵלַי יָפֶה (he treats me nicely). Another very common meaning is "to refer to / respond to": הַשָּׂר לֹא הִתְיַחֵס לַשְּׁאֵלָה (the minister did not address the question).

s.line: They kept this day as a holiday, then and ever after, and spent the time in feasting and dancing.
s.note: צִיֵּן = to mark (an occasion): צִיַּנּוּ אֶת יוֹם הַהֻלֶּדֶת שֶׁלּוֹ. It also means "to note, point out" and "to give a grade" (צִיּוּן = a grade at school). בִּלָּה = to spend time, usually enjoyably: בִּלִּינוּ בַּיָּם (we had a good time at the beach); בִּלּוּי = going out, entertainment.

s.line: “If our friends, the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, were only with us,” said the Lion, “I should be quite happy.”
s.note: אִלּוּ introduces an unreal condition (something that is not true now). The pattern is אִלּוּ + past tense, and then הָיִיתִי + participle for "I would": אִלּוּ הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי קוֹנֶה. In speech you'll also hear אִם used the same way. Here "quite" means "completely", so לְגַמְרֵי.

s.line: “Don’t you suppose we could rescue them?” asked the girl anxiously.
s.note: לְהַצִּיל = to rescue, save (hif'il, root נ־צ־ל). The noun הַצָּלָה (rescue) is this chapter's title; מַצִּיל is the lifeguard at the beach, and הַצִּילוּ! means "Help!". בִּדְאָגָה: בְּ + an abstract noun often works like an English adverb, as in בְּשִׂמְחָה (gladly) and בִּזְהִירוּת (carefully).

s.line: “We can try,” answered the Lion.
So they called the yellow Winkies and asked them if they would help to rescue their friends,

w: כָּל מַה שֶּׁבִּיכָלְתָּם|all in their power|~idiom: all that is in their ability
s.line: and the Winkies said that they would be delighted to do all in their power for Dorothy, who had set them free from bondage.
s.note: כָּל מַה שֶּׁבִּיכָלְתִּי = "all I can", from יְכֹלֶת (ability) + a possessive ending: אֶעֱשֶׂה כָּל מַה שֶּׁבִּיכָלְתִּי (I'll do everything I can). לְמַעַן = for the sake of, a little more formal than בִּשְׁבִיל: לְמַעַן הַיְּלָדִים. עַבְדוּת (slavery) is from the same root as עֶבֶד (slave) and עֲבוֹדָה (work).

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: So she chose a number of the Winkies who looked as if they knew the most, and they all started away.
s.note: בָּחַר בְּ: "to choose" takes בְּ in careful Hebrew (בָּחֲרָה בְּכַמָּה), though in speech you will often hear בָּחַר אֶת. בְּחִירוֹת = elections. כְּאִלּוּ = "as if", and in Israeli slang it is also a filler word, like English "like…".

w: מִיּוֹם הַמָּחֳרָת|of the next day|~lit. of the day of the morrow
s.line: They traveled that day and part of the next until they came to the rocky plain where the Tin Woodman lay,
s.note: שֶׁבּוֹ = "where", literally "that in it". Hebrew builds "where / in which" from שֶׁ plus a preposition with a pronoun that points back to the place: הַבַּיִת שֶׁבּוֹ גָּדַלְתִּי (the house I grew up in). יוֹם הַמָּחֳרָת = the following day; alone, לְמָחֳרָת = on the next day.

s.line: all battered and bent.
s.note: Two passive participles: מָעוּךְ (pa'ul form of pa'al מָעַךְ, to squash) and מְעֻקָּם (pu'al, from pi'el עִקֵּם, to bend out of shape). עָקֹם = crooked, and עִקֵּם אֶת הָאַף = "wrinkled his nose", i.e. showed distaste.

s.line: His axe was near him, but the blade was rusted and the handle broken off short.
The Winkies lifted him tenderly in their arms, and carried him back to the Yellow Castle again,
Dorothy shedding a few tears by the way at the sad plight of her old friend,
s.note: הִזִּיל דְּמָעוֹת = to shed tears, a fixed pair (hif'il of נ־ז־ל, as in נוֹזֵל, a liquid). לֹא הִזִּיל דִּמְעָה = "didn't shed a tear". וָתִיק = long-standing, veteran: חָבֵר וָתִיק (an old friend), עוֹבֵד וָתִיק (a senior employee). For a friend, "old" is וָתִיק, not זָקֵן.

s.line: and the Lion looking sober and sorry.
When they reached the castle Dorothy said to the Winkies:
“Are any of your people tinsmiths?”
s.note: פֶּחָח = a tinsmith, someone who works with פַּח (sheet metal). In Israel today the פֶּחָח is the auto-body man you take your car to after an accident, and his shop is a פֶּחָחוּת. בֵּינֵיכֶם = בֵּין + "you" (plural).

s.line: “Oh, yes.
Some of us are very good tinsmiths,” they told her.
“Then bring them to me,” she said.
s.note: תָּבִיאוּ is the future tense ("you will bring"), but in everyday speech the future is the normal, polite way to ask for something. The imperative הָבִיאוּ sounds stricter or more formal. Compare תָּבִיא לִי מַיִם (bring me some water).

s.line: And when the tinsmiths came, bringing with them all their tools in baskets, she inquired,
s.note: בָּאוּ (came) and הֵבִיאוּ (brought) are one root, ב־ו־א, in pa'al and hif'il: hif'il often means "make someone or something do the pa'al action", so "make come" = bring. כְּלִי (plural כֵּלִים) covers tools, dishes and instruments: כְּלֵי עֲבוֹדָה (work tools), כְּלֵי נְגִינָה (musical instruments).

s.line: “Can you straighten out those dents in the Tin Woodman, and bend him back into shape again, and solder him together where he is broken?”
s.note: מַכָּה = a blow, and also a dent in a car: יֵשׁ לִי מַכָּה בַּדֶּלֶת. A פֶּחָח literally "straightens dents" (מְיַשֵּׁר מַכּוֹת). לְהַלְחִים = to solder, הַלְחָמָה = soldering or welding. The root letters ל־ח־ם are also those of מִלְחָמָה (war) and לֶחֶם (bread): a good example of words that look alike without vowels.

w: טוֹב כְּמוֹ חָדָשׁ|as good as new|~idiom
s.line: The tinsmiths looked the Woodman over carefully and then answered that they thought they could mend him so he would be as good as ever.
s.note: לְדַעְתִּי = "in my opinion", from דַּעַת (knowledge, opinion) + a possessive ending: לְדַעְתְּךָ, לְדַעְתָּהּ, לְדַעְתָּם. It is one of the most useful words for giving an opinion. Notice also that Hebrew keeps the tense of the original speech (יְכוֹלִים, "can") where English shifts it back ("could").

w: נִגְּשׁוּ לָעֲבוֹדָה|set to work|~idiom: approached the work
s.line: So they set to work in one of the big yellow rooms of the castle and worked for three days and four nights,
s.note: אַרְבָּעָה לֵילוֹת: לַיְלָה ends in ה but is masculine (לַיְלָה טוֹב), so it takes the masculine number אַרְבָּעָה, just like שְׁלוֹשָׁה יָמִים. נִגַּשׁ (nif'al) = to approach: נִגַּשׁ לַחַלּוֹן. With a task it means "to set about": נִגְּשׁוּ לָעֲבוֹדָה.

s.line: hammering and twisting and bending and soldering and polishing and pounding at the legs and body and head of the Tin Woodman,
s.note: סוֹבֵב and כּוֹפֵף are pi'el of roots whose last two letters are the same (ס־ב־ב, כ־פ־ף). Such roots often make a pi'el with וֹ instead of a dagesh: סוֹבֵב, not סִבֵּב. סוֹבֵב is the everyday "to turn, rotate": סוֹבֵב אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ. דָּפַק = to knock or bang (דָּפַק בַּדֶּלֶת), and in slang it also means "to cheat someone".

s.line: until at last he was straightened out into his old form, and his joints worked as well as ever.
s.note: יֻשַּׁר is the pu'al (passive) of pi'el יִשֵּׁר (to straighten), which the tinsmiths were asked to do. Pi'el יִשֵּׁר → pu'al יֻשַּׁר, like תִּקֵּן → תֻּקַּן (was fixed). פָּעַל = to work or function (of a machine): הַמַּזְגָּן לֹא פּוֹעֵל (the air conditioner isn't working).

s.line: To be sure, there were several patches on him, but the tinsmiths did a good job,
and as the Woodman was not a vain man he did not mind the patches at all.
s.note: הִפְרִיעַ לְ = to bother or disturb someone, a very common verb: זֶה לֹא מַפְרִיעַ לִי (it doesn't bother me), סְלִיחָה שֶׁאֲנִי מַפְרִיעַ (sorry to interrupt). מִכֵּיוָן שֶׁ = "since, because", a bit more formal than כִּי. גַּנְדְּרָן is someone who fusses over his appearance.

s.line: When, at last, he walked into Dorothy’s room and thanked her for rescuing him, he was so pleased that he wept tears of joy,
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ… עַל = to thank someone (לְ) for something (עַל). It is hif'il of י־ד־ה, the root of תּוֹדָה. Before a whole clause, עַל becomes עַל שֶׁ: תּוֹדָה עַל שֶׁבָּאתָ (thanks for coming). The same verb also means "to admit": הוּא הוֹדָה בָּאַשְׁמָה (he admitted guilt).

s.line: and Dorothy had to wipe every tear carefully from his face with her apron, so his joints would not be rusted.
s.note: הֶחֱלִיד = "to rust", hif'il, used without an object (הַבֹּרֶג הֶחֱלִיד, the screw rusted). The result is the pa'ul form חָלוּד (rusty), and the noun is חֲלוּדָה (rust). כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that": דַּבֵּר לְאַט כְּדֵי שֶׁאָבִין.

w: מֵרֹב שִׂמְחָה|from sheer joy|~idiom: from much joy
s.line: At the same time her own tears fell thick and fast at the joy of meeting her old friend again,
s.note: מֵרֹב + noun = "from so much …", giving the cause: מֵרֹב עֲיֵפוּת (from sheer tiredness), לֹא יָכֹלְתִּי לִישֹׁן מֵרֹב הִתְרַגְּשׁוּת (I couldn't sleep from excitement). זָלְגוּ: tears "trickle" (זָלַג). דְּמָעוֹת זוֹלְגוֹת is the standard phrase.

s.line: and these tears did not need to be wiped away.
As for the Lion, he wiped his eyes so often with the tip of his tail that it became quite wet,
s.note: אֲשֶׁר לְ = "as for, regarding", a formal phrase you'll meet in the news and in official letters: אֲשֶׁר לַתַּקְצִיב, … (as for the budget, …). In conversation people say לְגַבֵּי or וּמָה עִם… נִהְיָה = became: נִהְיָה קַר (it got cold).

s.line: and he was obliged to go out into the courtyard and hold it in the sun till it dried.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ = "was forced, had to", nif'al of א־ל־ץ, very common in speech and news: נֶאֱלַצְתִּי לְבַטֵּל (I had to cancel), הַמָּטוֹס נֶאֱלַץ לִנְחֹת (the plane was forced to land). הִתְיַבֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to dry out by itself; יִבֵּשׁ (pi'el) = to dry something, and מְיַבֵּשׁ is a dryer.

s.line: “If we only had the Scarecrow with us again,” said the Tin Woodman, when Dorothy had finished telling him everything that had happened, “I should be quite happy.”
s.note: סִיֵּם + infinitive = to finish doing something: סִיַּמְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל. Hebrew has no past perfect: "had finished" and "had happened" are plain past (סִיְּמָה, קָרָה), and אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ makes the order clear.

s.line: “We must try to find him,” said the girl.
So she called the Winkies to help her,
and they walked all that day and part of the next until they came to the tall tree in the branches of which the Winged Monkeys had tossed the Scarecrow’s clothes.
s.note: הָעֵץ שֶׁעַל הָעֲנָפִים שֶׁלּוֹ = "the tree onto whose branches", literally "the tree that on its branches". Hebrew has no word for "whose" or "of which": it uses שֶׁ and then a pronoun (שֶׁלּוֹ) pointing back to the noun. Compare הָאִישׁ שֶׁהַבַּיִת שֶׁלּוֹ נִשְׂרַף (the man whose house burned down).

s.line: It was a very tall tree, and the trunk was so smooth that no one could climb it;
s.note: טִפֵּס עַל = to climb (up) something, with עַל: לְטַפֵּס עַל הַר. טִפּוּס is climbing as a sport (קִיר טִפּוּס, a climbing wall). גֶּזַע = tree trunk, and also "race" or "breed": כֶּלֶב גֶּזַע (a purebred dog).

s.line: but the Woodman said at once, “I’ll chop it down, and then we can get the Scarecrow’s clothes.”
s.note: כָּרַת = to cut down (a tree): כְּרִיתַת יְעָרוֹת = deforestation. It also appears in the fixed phrase כָּרַת בְּרִית (made a covenant or alliance). הוֹרִיד (hif'il of יָרַד, to go down) = "to bring/take down", and in modern use also "to download": הוֹרַדְתִּי אֶת הַקֹּבֶץ.

s.line: Now while the tinsmiths had been at work mending the Woodman himself, another of the Winkies, who was a goldsmith, had made an axe-handle of solid gold and fitted it to the Woodman’s axe, instead of the old broken handle.

s.note: One root, two binyanim: תִּקֵּן (pi'el) = to repair, and הִתְקִין (hif'il) = to install or fit. הִתְקַנְתִּי אַפְּלִיקַצְיָה = I installed an app; תִּקַּנְתִּי אֶת הָאוֹפַנַּיִם = I fixed the bike. תִּקּוּן = a repair, הַתְקָנָה = installation. צוֹרֵף is a goldsmith or jeweler.

s.line: Others polished the blade until all the rust was removed and it glistened like burnished silver.
s.note: Two passives here. הוּסְרָה is hof'al, the passive of hif'il הֵסִיר (to remove): הַשֶּׁלֶט הוּסַר (the sign was removed). מְלֻטָּשׁ is the pu'al participle of pi'el לִטֵּשׁ (to polish), as in יַהֲלוֹם מְלֻטָּשׁ (a cut diamond). מַבְרִיק (shining) also means "brilliant": רַעְיוֹן מַבְרִיק.

s.line: As soon as he had spoken, the Tin Woodman began to chop,
s.note: בְּרֶגַע שֶׁ = "as soon as", literally "at the moment that": תִּתְקַשֵּׁר בְּרֶגַע שֶׁאַתָּה מַגִּיעַ (call as soon as you arrive). After a time word at the start, Hebrew often puts the verb before the subject: הִתְחִיל אִישׁ הַפַּח.

s.line: and in a short time the tree fell over with a crash,
whereupon the Scarecrow’s clothes fell out of the branches and rolled off on the ground.
s.note: הִתְגַּלְגֵּל = to roll (by itself), hitpa'el of the four-letter root ג־ל־ג־ל, as in גַּלְגַּל (wheel). The idiom אֵיךְ שֶׁהַדְּבָרִים הִתְגַּלְגְּלוּ means "how things turned out".

s.line: Dorothy picked them up and had the Winkies carry them back to the castle,
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־ = to ask someone (to do something). The person you ask takes מִן: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ לַעֲזֹר (I asked him to help). For asking a question, use שָׁאַל אֶת. בְּבַקָּשָׁה (please) is from the same root.

s.line: where they were stuffed with nice, clean straw;
s.note: מֻלְּאוּ = "were filled/stuffed", pu'al (passive) of pi'el מִלֵּא (to fill). Its participle מְמֻלָּא is the kitchen word for "stuffed": פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא (stuffed pepper). Pi'el מִלֵּא טֹפֶס = to fill in a form.

w: טוֹב כְּמוֹ חָדָשׁ|as good as new|~idiom
s.line: and behold! here was the Scarecrow, as good as ever, thanking them over and over again for saving him.
s.note: וְהִנֵּה = "and look! / and there it was", used in storytelling to present a surprise: פָּתַחְתִּי אֶת הַדֶּלֶת, וְהִנֵּה…. שׁוּב וָשׁוּב = again and again. Note the וָ with qamats, kept in this fixed pair, as in יוֹם וָלַיְלָה.

s.line: Now that they were reunited, Dorothy and her friends spent a few happy days at the Yellow Castle,

w: יִהְיֶה לָהֶם נוֹחַ|they would be comfortable|~lit. it will be comfortable to them
s.line: where they found everything they needed to make them comfortable.
s.note: נוֹחַ לִי = "I'm comfortable", literally "it is comfortable to me": the person goes after לְ, as with קַר לִי and חַם לִי. Ask a guest נוֹחַ לְךָ? (are you comfortable?). The same word describes things: כִּסֵּא נוֹחַ (a comfortable chair).

s.line: But one day the girl thought of Aunt Em,
s.note: נִזְכַּר בְּ = to remember, to think of suddenly (nif'al, with בְּ): פִּתְאֹם נִזְכַּרְתִּי בְּמַשֶּׁהוּ. זָכַר (pa'al) means to remember in general, הִזְכִּיר (hif'il) means to remind or mention, and תִּזְכֹּרֶת is a reminder on your phone.

s.line: and said, “We must go back to Oz, and claim his promise.”
s.note: קִיֵּם הַבְטָחָה = to keep a promise (pi'el of ק־ו־ם). The opposite is הֵפֵר הַבְטָחָה (broke a promise). קִיֵּם also means "to hold" an event, a very common news usage: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה קִיְּמָה יְשִׁיבָה (the government held a meeting). דָּרַשׁ = to demand; דְּרִישָׁה = a demand or requirement.

s.line: “Yes,” said the Woodman, “at last I shall get my heart.”
“And I shall get my brains,” added the Scarecrow joyfully.
s.note: הוֹסִיף = to add (hif'il of י־ס־ף). As a speech verb it means "added (in speech)", just as in English. Related: תּוֹסֶפֶת (an addition or side dish), and נוֹסָף (additional), as in עוֹד פְּרָטִים נוֹסָפִים.

s.line: “And I shall get my courage,” said the Lion thoughtfully.
s.note: מְהֻרְהָר = thoughtful, lost in thought: a pu'al participle of the four-letter root ה־ר־ה־ר (pi'el הִרְהֵר, to ponder, muse). Hebrew often uses an adjective describing the speaker where English uses an adverb: אָמַר מְהֻרְהָר, "said (being) thoughtful". הִרְהוּרִים = musings, second thoughts.

w: וּמָחֲאָה כַּפַּיִם|and clapped her hands|~idiom: struck palms
s.line: “And I shall get back to Kansas,” cried Dorothy, clapping her hands.
s.note: מָחָא כַּפַּיִם = to clap (literally "struck palms"); the noun is מְחִיאוֹת כַּפַּיִם = applause. כַּף יָד is the palm of the hand, and כַּפַּיִם is its dual form ("two palms").

s.line: “Oh, let us start for the Emerald City tomorrow!”
s.note: בּוֹא / בּוֹאוּ + a "we" future = "let's": בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ (let's go), בּוֹא נִרְאֶה (let's see). This is the everyday way to make a suggestion. יָצָא לְ = to set out for a place.

s.line: This they decided to do.
The next day they called the Winkies together and bade them good-bye.
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ־ = to say goodbye to, part from (nif'al of פ־ר־ד): נִפְרַדְנוּ בַּשָּׂדֶה (we said goodbye at the airport). It also means "to break up" (הֵם נִפְרְדוּ). From the same root: נִפְרָד (separate) and פְּרֵדָה (a parting).

s.line: The Winkies were sorry to have them go,
s.note: הִצְטַעֵר = to be sorry, regret. It is hitpa'el, but when the root begins with צ the ת moves after it and turns into ט: הִתְ + צ־ע־ר → הִצְטַעֵר. The present מִצְטַעֵר / מִצְטַעֶרֶת is the everyday "I'm sorry".

s.line: and they had grown so fond of the Tin Woodman that they begged him to stay and rule over them and the Yellow Land of the West.
s.note: הִתְחַנֵּן לִפְנֵי = to beg, plead with someone, literally "before" them: הוּא הִתְחַנֵּן לְפָנַי שֶׁאַגִּיד כֵּן. מָלַךְ עַל = to reign over; the king is the מֶלֶךְ. After verbs of asking and begging, שֶׁ + future is the normal pattern: שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר (that he stay).

s.line: Finding they were determined to go, the Winkies gave Toto and the Lion each a golden collar;
s.note: נֶחְרָץ = determined, firm, decisive. It's common in the news: הַכְחָשָׁה נֶחְרֶצֶת (a flat denial), בְּאֹפֶן נֶחְרָץ (firmly). In conversation you might say הֶחְלִיטוּ סוֹפִית (they made up their minds) instead. קוֹלָר is the everyday word for a dog's collar.

s.line: and to Dorothy they presented a beautiful bracelet studded with diamonds;
s.note: הֶעֱנִיק = to grant, award, present, more formal than נָתַן: הֶעֱנִיקוּ לוֹ פְּרָס (he was awarded a prize). מְשֻׁבָּץ = set, inlaid (pu'al of pi'el שִׁבֵּץ). In modern use שִׁבֵּץ also means "to place, schedule, assign": שִׁבְּצוּ אוֹתִי בַּמִּשְׁמֶרֶת שֶׁל הַבֹּקֶר (they put me on the morning shift).

s.line: and to the Scarecrow they gave a gold-headed walking stick, to keep him from stumbling;

w: וּלְאִישׁ הַפַּח|and to the Tin Woodman
s.line: and to the Tin Woodman they offered a silver oil-can, inlaid with gold and set with precious jewels.
s.note: הִגִּישׁ = to hand over, present, serve (hif'il of נ־ג־שׁ, the root of נִגַּשׁ, to approach): הַמֶּלְצַר הִגִּישׁ אֶת הַמָּנָה (the waiter served the dish). In offices and the news it means "to submit": הִגִּישׁ בַּקָּשָׁה (submitted an application). מְעֻטָּר = decorated (pu'al), from the root of עֲטָרָה (crown).

s.line: Every one of the travelers made the Winkies a pretty speech in return,
s.note: נָשָׂא נְאוּם = to make or give a speech, the standard phrase (literally "carried a speech"): רֹאשׁ הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה נָשָׂא נְאוּם. נָשָׂא has many meanings: to carry, to bear, and in נָשָׂא אִשָּׁה, to marry.

s.line: and all shook hands with them until their arms ached.
s.note: לָחַץ יָד = to shake hands ("pressed a hand"), with עִם: לָחַצְנוּ יָדַיִם. לָחַץ alone means to press or pressure, and לַחַץ is stress: אֲנִי בְּלַחַץ (I'm stressed).

s.line: Dorothy went to the Witch’s cupboard to fill her basket with food for the journey,
and there she saw the Golden Cap.
She tried it on her own head and found that it fitted her exactly.
s.note: מָדַד = to measure, and also to try on clothes: אֶפְשָׁר לִמְדֹּד? (can I try it on?), תָּא מְדִידָה (fitting room). מַתְאִים לְ = fits, suits: זֶה מַתְאִים לָךְ (it suits you), and with a time or plan, מָחָר מַתְאִים לְךָ? (does tomorrow work for you?).

s.line: She did not know anything about the charm of the Golden Cap,

w: כּוֹבַע הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ|the sunbonnet|~lit. hat of the sun
s.line: but she saw that it was pretty, so she made up her mind to wear it and carry her sunbonnet in the basket.
s.note: Hebrew has different verbs for "wear": חָבַשׁ for a hat or helmet (חָבַשׁ כּוֹבַע), לָבַשׁ for clothes, נָעַל for shoes, and הִרְכִּיב for glasses. חָבַשׁ also means "to bandage", and a חוֹבֵשׁ is an army medic.

s.line: Then, being prepared for the journey, they all started for the Emerald City;
s.note: מוּכָן = ready, a hof'al participle ("made ready"), the passive of hif'il הֵכִין (to prepare): הָאֹכֶל מוּכָן (the food is ready), אַתָּה מוּכָן? (are you ready?). לְעֵבֶר = toward, a bit more literary than לְכִוּוּן.

s.line: and the Winkies gave them three cheers and many good wishes to carry with them.
s.note: אִחֵל לְ = to wish someone something (pi'el), with the person after לְ: אֲנִי מְאַחֵל לְךָ הַצְלָחָה (I wish you success); אִחוּלִים = wishes, as in אִחוּלֵי הַחְלָמָה (get-well wishes). הֵרִיעַ לְ = to cheer for someone, from the root of תְּרוּעָה (a loud blast or shout).
